extracted.intended_audience: researchers in digital libraries and computational linguistics, and scholars of citation analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical corpus-linguistic analysis of citation language to identify linguistic structures that characterize citation functions (supporting, disputing, mentioning). Uses large pre-classified citation corpora to derive theory and guidance for modeling citation function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation type taxonomy (supporting, disputing, mentioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation classes used in the study are supporting, disputing, and mentioning citations (2 million citations from each class drawn from the scite Smart Citation dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these three categories as the target citation functions when analyzing language; ensure large, balanced samples per class for comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify statistically significant linguistic structures per citation class
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking for linguistic structures that characterize distinct classes of citations for the purposes of understanding the intent and function of a citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corpus-linguistic methods (e.g., collocate analysis, statistical significance testing) and generate comparison tables to reveal unique, statistically significant language structures belonging to each citation type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on sentiment as a predictor of citation function
rubrics_metrics.description: Within citation collocates, there is very low correlation between citation type and sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use sentiment of collocates as a primary feature for predicting citation function; sentiment signals are poor predictors according to the corpus findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpreting citations as expressions of opinion due to low subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjectivity of citation collocates across classes is very low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because collocate subjectivity is low, an opinion-expressing mode of understanding citations (implicit in previous citation sentiment analysis literature) is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualize citations as claims-making devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations can be better understood as claims-making devices where the citation type can be explained by understanding how two claims are being compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame analyses around how the citing text and cited claim are compared or contrasted (claims comparison) rather than treating citations primarily as expressions of sentiment or subjective opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use large pre-classified citation corpora for empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a large sample of a pre-classified citation corpus (the study uses 2 million citations per class from scite Smart Citation dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on big, pre-labeled citation corpora to provide robust empirical bases for corpus-linguistic analyses and to enable detection of statistically significant patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform corpus linguistic analysis prior to predictive feature modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous works focused on modeling linguistic features first and drew conclusions about language structures from classifier performance or inter-annotator agreement; this study instead begins with corpus-linguistic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct descriptive and comparative corpus studies to surface candidate linguistic structures and patterns before building classifiers or drawing conclusions from modeling performance or IAA metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate comparison tables to surface unique features per citation type
rubrics_metrics.description: By generating comparison tables for each citation type the study presents linguistic features that uniquely characterize each type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabular comparisons of collocates, frequencies, and statistical measures across classes to identify distinguishing linguistic markers and to support interpretation.
